newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada police get Bre-X fraud complaint.
newsitem.headline: Canada police get Bre-X fraud complaint.

text.p: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said on Wednesday they had received a fraud complaint from embattled Bre-X Minerals Ltd. as investors tallied up their losses from history's biggest gold swindle.
Investigators were meeting to decide their next move in a widening probe over the Bre-X gold fiasco, but there were no plans yet to send a team to Indonesia, an RCMP official said.

The Busang discovery in Indonesia -- touted by Calgary, Alberta-based Bre-X as the richest gold find of the century -- was falsified on a scale "without precedent in the history of mining," according to a report by consultant Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd. released late Sunday.
Bre-X officials were unavailable to comment on Wednesday.

"They gave us the Strathcona report and the letter of complaint. Now we're in meetings to discuss which direction to take from there," Deleen Schoff, a spokeswoman for the RCMP in Alberta, said in a telephone interview.
Schoff denied a report from Indonesian police on Wednesday that an RCMP team would arrive in Jakarta either on Thursday or Friday to question people involved in the Busang affair.
"At this point anything is possible, but we haven't designated anyone to go over (to Indonesia)," Schoff said. "We haven't decided if we're going over."
She said Bre-X's letter of complaint to the RCMP, which was signed by Chief Executive David Walsh, claimed "that they were defrauded. They don't identify anyone," Schoff said.
"The (RCMP) people who are in meetings have the letter. They're discussing it right now," she said.

The Alberta government has named a special prosecutor, Terry Matchett, to work with the RCMP in its Bre-X probe. Matchett is director of Alberta's special prosecutions branch, which specialises in commercial crime.
"He'll work very closely with the police, assisting them and providing them with legal advice," Leslie Gronow, a spokeswoman for Alberta's Justice Ministry, said.
Gronow said there were no immediate plans for Matchett to go to Indonesia, "but that may occur later."
While police met over the Busang embroglio, there was increasing speculation over how much and when Bre-X officials knew about the tampering of core samples from Busang.
Strathcona said in its report that there were several red flags contained in reports that Bre-X received last year from Canada's Kilborn SNC-Lavalin Inc. and Australia's Normet Pty Ltd.
Strathcona concluded Bre-X's storage warehouse near the Borneo town of Samarinda, where core samples were kept for a lengthy period of time, was the most likely spot for any tampering.
Published reports from Indonesia have quoted local Bre-X employees as saying that they blended reddish, white and gold-coloured powders with pulverized rock samples from Busang.
Analysts said senior Bre-X officials either did not recognise or ignored the clues contained in the Kilborn and Normet reports.

Before Sunday's announcement, Walsh, the Bre-X CEO, had dismissed doubts about Busang that had dogged his company since March. He said he was shocked by Strathcona's report and had hired investigators to find the culprits.
Bre-X's chief of exploration, John Felderhof, also has expressed dismay over the tampering at Busang and denied any knowledge of the fraud.

Rumours about Busang began circulating in March when Bre-X's chief geologist at the Busang site, Michael de Guzman, allegedly jumped to his death from a helicopter while flying to a meeting in Indonesia.
On March 26, Bre-X partner Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc., a big mining company based in New Orleans, said that its preliminary tests found "insignificant" amounts of gold.
After the Freeport announcement, Bre-X immediately hired Strathcona to review its Busang project.
The developments sparked panic selling of Bre-X shares, wiping almost C$3 billion ($2.1 billion) from the company's market value when the stock plummeted to C$2.50 ($1.80) from around C$15 ($11).

In the wake of Strathcona's bombshell Sunday Bre-X's stock -- once worth more than C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) -- collapsed to pennies a share on Tuesday. The stock was trading flat at C0.09 cents a share on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Wednesday.
Freeport and an Indonesian company said on Monday they were withdrawing from the Busang project.
